A.biggest_strength: A cohesive dark-mode aesthetic with an intuitive color-coding system linking parameters, arguments, and return expressions to their call stack frames.
A.biggest_weakness: Superficial multi-language coverage where languages only swap a function name, compounded by unreadable mobile scaling and a lack of granular stepping controls.
factual_errors: The caption claims that each code snippet was run with its real tool (python3, node, gcc, java, rustc, ruby) and prints 25, but the C, Rust, and Java snippets contain top-level executable statements outside any function or class and fail to compile with gcc, rustc, and javac as written.

The call stack displays a 'main' frame for all languages, even though Python, JavaScript, and Ruby do not define or use a 'main' function in the code or their runtime environments (using module scope, global execution context, or top-level main object).

At step 12, the explainer claims that 'the call site prints 25; the stack is empty' and wipes the stack, ignoring that printing (e.g. print, printf) is itself a function call that allocates a frame while the caller frame remains active.
The explainer purports to demonstrate how calls work across different languages, but the execution model and stack dynamics are 100% identical; switching languages only renames 'sum_sq' to 'sumSq'.

B.biggest_strength: Exceptional technical depth and genuine cross-language breadth, pairing interactive code and stack visualizers with accurate ABI, bytecode, and runtime execution details across 14 languages.
B.biggest_weakness: The visual presentation of the call stack uses a utilitarian box layout rather than animated value tokens moving directly into code lines.
factual_errors: Minor text discrepancy: the header states 'One small program, 13 languages', but the interface provides 14 selectable options (13 high-level languages plus x86-64 assembly).
